properties.notes: Tarquinii ranked among the twelve cities of the Etruscan League and gave Rome its last royal dynasty, the Tarquins. Its hilltop circuit walls and the sprawling Ara della Regina temple, once the largest in Etruria at 77 by 34 meters, still stood in ruin under Roman rule. Terracotta winged horses from that temple's pediment counted among Etruscan art's finest survivals. By 117 CE the city had long been a quiet Roman municipium living in the shadow of its own monuments.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, photo of the Ara della Regina temple ruins at Tarquinia

properties.modern_location: Isola Farnese, near Formello, Lazio, Italy
properties.notes: Veii was Rome's closest Etruscan rival, holding out through a ten-year siege before Marcus Furius Camillus finally razed it in 396 BCE. Its Portonaccio sanctuary once displayed the life-size terracotta Apollo of Veii, a masterwork attributed to the sculptor Vulca. By 117 CE the site carried Emperor Augustus's small colonial town, Municipium Augustum Veiens, built directly over the vanished Etruscan capital's foundations.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Apollo of Veii terracotta statue from the Portonaccio sanctuary

properties.notes: Caere ranked as one of the wealthiest Etruscan cities, its aristocrats buried under stone tumuli so grand that Rome once entrusted it with safekeeping sacred relics during the Gallic sack of 390 BCE. The famous terracotta Sarcophagus of the Spouses, sculpted around 520 BCE, came from its cemeteries. Rome absorbed Caere as a voteless civitas after 273 BCE, and by 117 CE it survived as a quiet municipium overshadowed by its own necropolis.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Sarcophagus of the Spouses from Villa Giulia in Rome.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Sarcophagus of the Spouses from Caere, Villa Giulia, Rome

properties.notes: Vulci controlled a stretch of the Tyrrhenian coast and grew rich exporting bronzework across the Mediterranean before Rome crushed it in 280 BCE. The François Tomb, painted with scenes of Roman legend, was cut into its necropolis rock. A bridge still spans the Fiora gorge on foundations the Etruscans first laid, later nicknamed the Devil's Bridge for its high arches. By 117 CE the once-mighty city was scattered ruins around a working river crossing.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, ruins at the Vulci archaeological park

properties.notes: Populonia was the only major Etruscan city built directly on the sea, its furnaces smelting Elban iron ore into a fortune that funded its acropolis and walls. Slag heaps from that industry still ringed the bay in Roman times. The city sided with Marius and paid for it with a Sullan sack around 80 BCE, leaving it a shrunken hill town by the time of Trajan. Its acropolis walls remained visible landmarks in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Rocca di Populonia on the ancient acropolis site

properties.notes: Rusellae's massive polygonal-block walls, over three kilometers around, ranked among the best-preserved Etruscan fortifications anywhere, still standing centuries after Rome conquered the city in 294 BCE. Romans folded it into their own grid, adding a forum, baths, and an amphitheater cut into the hillside. A visitor in 117 CE would have walked past genuinely Etruscan masonry supporting a thoroughly Roman town.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Etruscan walls of Rusellae

properties.modern_location: Vetulonia, near Castiglione della Pescaia, Tuscany, Italy
properties.notes: Vetulonia minted some of the earliest coinage in Etruria and, by Roman tradition, supplied the fasces and curule chairs that became symbols of Roman magisterial power. Its Orientalizing-era tumulus tombs, including the Tomba del Diavolino with its long stone dromos, held gold rivaling Cerveteri's finds. A stretch of sixth-century BCE Arce walls still crowned the hilltop in Roman times, though the town itself had shrunk to little by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Tomba del Diavolino II at Vetulonia

properties.notes: Clusium's King Lars Porsena marched on Rome around 508 BCE, a campaign Roman legend later spun into tales of heroic resistance rather than admitted defeat. The city's rock-cut tombs, like the Tomba della Pellegrina, still held carved sarcophagi and cinerary urns under Roman rule. Clusium also gave the world the François Vase, a Greek krater so prized it was buried with its owner. By 117 CE it was an ordinary Roman town living beside its own funerary chambers.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Tomba della Pellegrina near Chiusi

properties.notes: Perusia counted among the twelve cities of the Etruscan League and later became the last holdout against Octavian in the Perusine War of 41 to 40 BCE, a siege that ended with the city burned. Its Etruscan travertine walls survived the fire well enough that Augustus restored one gate and renamed it Porta Augusta. That gate, carved with shield reliefs, still framed the road into the rebuilt town in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Etruscan Arch (Arco Etrusco / Porta Augusta) of Perugia

properties.notes: Cortona sat among the twelve cities of the Etruscan League on a hilltop above the Val di Chiana, ringed by three kilometers of massive sandstone walls raised in the fourth century BCE. On the plain below, aristocratic families built tumulus tombs nicknamed meloni for their rounded shape, the largest over fifty meters across. The Porta Bifora, a rare double-arched gate, still controlled entry in 117 CE, its walls and tombs standing largely undisturbed under Roman rule.

Faesulae was a major hill-fort of northern Etruria and briefly a rebel base for Catiline's conspirators in 62 BCE. Its Etruscan temple, first raised in the late fourth century BCE, burned down and was rebuilt on the same footprint under Augustus, so the sanctuary a visitor saw in 117 CE stood on genuinely pre-Roman foundations. The city's Etruscan wall circuit still enclosed the northern edge of the town, and Florence in the valley below had yet to eclipse it.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Etrusco-Roman temple ruins at Fiesole

properties.notes: Volaterrae ruled a large inland territory as one of the twelve cities of the Etruscan League and kept minting its own coinage into the Roman period. Its Porta all'Arco gate, jambs carved in the fourth century BCE with three weathered stone heads set in the arch, still stood at the southern approach. The town backed Marius against Sulla and endured a two-year siege before surrendering around 80 BCE. By 117 CE it was a settled municipium wrapped inside its Etruscan founders' walls.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Porta all'Arco, the Etruscan gate of Volterra

properties.notes: Volsinii was one of the twelve Etruscan League cities and, by the majority scholarly view used here, occupied the volcanic plateau of modern Orvieto rather than nearby Bolsena, a matter still argued in scholarship. Rome destroyed the city in 264 BCE after crushing a slave revolt among its own aristocracy, then resettled the population at Bolsena. The rock-cut Crocifisso del Tufo necropolis, laid out in a grid of inscribed doorways, survived that destruction intact.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Crocifisso del Tufo necropolis at Orvieto

properties.notes: Pyrgi served as the busy harbor of Caere and hosted a sanctuary sacred enough that Phoenician traders left offerings there beside Etruscans. Excavators in 1964 found three inscribed gold tablets buried near Temple B, a bilingual dedication from around 500 BCE by Caere's ruler Thefarie Velianas linking the goddess Uni to Phoenician Astarte. Rome sacked the port in 384 BCE and later planted a colony on the spot, but the temple foundations remained visible ruins through the imperial period.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Pyrgi gold tablets found at the sanctuary

properties.notes: Spina thrived from the sixth to third centuries BCE as an Etruscan gateway to the Adriatic, trading so heavily with Greece its graves yielded more fine Attic pottery than almost anywhere outside Greece. Built on timber piles over the marshy Po delta, the city was swallowed as the river's silt advanced. By Trajan's reign the port had been gone for centuries, and it stayed hidden until 1922 land-reclamation work uncovered its necropolis.

Kainua was a showcase of Etruscan city planning north of the Apennines, laid out around 500 BCE on a strict grid with fifteen-meter avenues crossing narrower streets at right angles. Celtic Gauls swept through the Po valley in the fourth century BCE, and the city was abandoned by roughly 350 BCE, its grid frozen rather than built over. That abandonment is why archaeologists prize the site today, but it also means no standing city remained there for anyone to see in 117 CE.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Marzabotto citt%C3%A0 etrusca nei pressi della plateia D.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the excavated street grid of Kainua at Marzabotto

properties.modern_location: Campo della Fiera, near Orvieto, Umbria, Italy
properties.notes: Fanum Voltumnae served as the federal sanctuary of the Etruscan League, where delegates from all twelve cities gathered yearly for games and to elect a shared leader. Its location went unconfirmed until excavations starting in 2000 at Campo della Fiera, below Orvieto, uncovered temple foundations, a sacred road, and a terracotta deity's head favoring this site over rivals. The sanctuary stayed in cult use, with a temple rebuilt there as late as the first century CE.

Monterozzi held roughly six thousand graves cut into the hillside east of Tarquinia, around two hundred painted with frescoes of banquets, dancers, and hunts dating back to the seventh century BCE. The Tomb of the Augurs, decorated around 520 BCE, preserved some of the earliest fully painted Etruscan tomb interiors known. Sealed underground rather than looted, the chambers kept their vivid color through Roman rule; a visitor in 117 CE would have seen only unmarked mounds above ground.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Phersu from the painted walls of the tomb of the Augurs at Tarquinia, 525-500 BCE, Etruscan.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, fresco from the Tomb of the Augurs, Monterozzi necropolis

properties.notes: Banditaccia was Caere's great city of the dead, laid out with streets and neighborhoods of round tumulus tombs cut from soft volcanic tufa, some over 40 meters across. Wealthy families carved tomb interiors to mimic real houses, complete with stone beds, pillars, and household objects rendered in relief. Burials had continued there since the ninth century BCE, so its monumental character was already centuries old by the time Trajan ruled, and its scale later helped earn it UNESCO recognition.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, tufa tumulus tombs at the Banditaccia necropolis

properties.notes: Norchia's tombs were carved straight into cliff faces along the old Via Clodia, an unusual choice for Etruscans who typically preferred underground chambers or freestanding tumuli. Facade tombs shaped like miniature temples, some with false doors chiseled directly from the rock, date mainly to the Hellenistic fourth through second centuries BCE. The town above never grew into a major Roman settlement, leaving the cliffside tombs standing recognizable through the Roman era.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, rock-cut facade tomb at Norchia

properties.notes: Sovana's necropolis cut its grandest tomb, the temple-fronted Tomba Ildebranda, directly from soft tufa cliffs in the third or second century BCE, with carved columns imitating real Hellenistic architecture. Older chamber tombs date back to the seventh century BCE, linked by deep sunken roadways still called vie cave. The necropolis lay outside the small Roman-era town of Suana and was never built over, its rock-cut monuments still visible to anyone passing through in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, Tomba Ildebranda at the Sovana necropolis

properties.modern_location: Gulf of Baratti, near Populonia, Tuscany, Italy
properties.notes: The Baratti necropolis served Populonia's ironworking elite, its grandest grave the Tomba dei Carri, a chariot burial mound 28 meters across dating to the seventh century BCE. Family tumuli sat alongside smaller shrine-shaped aedicule tombs, many built atop layers of slag from the smelting works that made the city rich. Roman-era burials continued nearby even after Etruscan Populonia's peak had passed, and by 117 CE the older monumental tombs still stood as fading markers of that wealth.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, tumulus tomb at the Baratti necropolis, Populonia

properties.notes: Byrsa served as Carthage's citadel, holding a temple to Eshmun and, by legend, the hill Dido won by cutting an oxhide into a thread thin enough to encircle it. Rome razed the Punic quarter in 146 BCE, and when Augustus's colonists rebuilt Carthage they leveled the summit and buried the Punic ruins under an artificial terrace to raise a new forum. By 117 CE a visitor standing on Byrsa saw Roman civic buildings, unaware a six-story Punic neighborhood lay sealed beneath their feet.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the excavated Punic Quarter atop Byrsa Hill, Carthage

properties.notes: Utica predated Carthage itself, founded by Tyrian colonists and traditionally reckoned the first Phoenician settlement in North Africa. The city stayed loyal to Rome through the Punic Wars, opening its gates in 149 BCE and earning free-city status while Carthage burned. Cato the Younger chose to die there in 46 BCE rather than live under Caesar. By 117 CE Utica ranked among Africa Proconsularis's leading cities.

Kerkouane was a working Punic town abandoned during the First Punic War around 250 BCE and pillaged after Rome took nearby Aspis; unlike Carthage or Utica, it was never resettled. Its streets, pink-mortar bathtubs, workshops, and ramparts sat undisturbed under drifting sand for two thousand years until a 1952 rediscovery. It is the only Phoenicio-Punic city known to survive without a later town built on top, and by 117 CE it had already lain buried for over three centuries.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, ruins of the Punic town of Kerkouane

properties.notes: Meninx began as a Phoenician trading post on Djerba and grew into one of the Mediterranean's great purple-dye centers, ranking behind only Tyre by Pliny the Elder's account. Workers crushed murex and purpura shellfish by the ton in stone vats, and shell middens from that industry still ring the site. Rome made Meninx the administrative capital of Djerba, already prosperous by 117 CE, decades before its second- and third-century building boom.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the archaeological site of Meninx, Djerba

properties.modern_location: San Pantaleo Island, Stagnone Lagoon, near Marsala, Sicily, Italy
properties.notes: Motya was Carthage's principal naval stronghold on Sicily until Dionysius I of Syracuse besieged it in 397 BCE with the era's newest siege engines, crucifying defenders who survived the sack. Survivors resettled at newly founded Lilybaeum, and Motya was never rebuilt. Excavations later recovered the marble Motya Charioteer, a Greek masterwork found on Carthaginian soil. By 117 CE the island had sat empty for over five centuries.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The Motya Charioteer, made by a Greek sculptor in Sicily, about 460-450 BC, found in 1979 on the Sicilian island of Motya (Mozia), Winning at the ancient Games, British Museum (7642730456).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Motya Charioteer, found on the island in 1979 (photographed at the British Museum)

properties.modern_location: Monte Catalfano, Santa Flavia, near Palermo, Sicily, Italy
properties.notes: Solus was one of only three major Phoenician strongholds Sicily's Greek colonization left standing, alongside Panormus and Motya. Enemies destroyed the original lowland settlement around 397 BCE, and survivors rebuilt higher on Monte Catalfano's slopes. Rome absorbed Solus peacefully during the First Punic War, and the rebuilt hill town, with houses like the mosaic-floored Casa di Leda, remained a functioning municipium through Trajan's reign.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the House of Garlands at Solunto

properties.notes: Panormus began as a Phoenician colony called Ziz, "flower," around the 8th century BCE, and grew alongside Motya and Solus into one of Carthage's three principal Sicilian strongholds. Its buried necropolis, first uncovered in 1746 and still being excavated as recently as 2004, has yielded more than seven hundred graves cut between the late 7th and early 3rd centuries BCE. Rome took the city in 254 BCE, and by 117 CE the old Phoenician cemetery lay forgotten underground beneath a thriving Roman Panormus.

Phoenician settlers reached this volcanic island by the late 8th century BCE, and Carthage later took direct control, minting its own coins stamped with a goddess's head, likely Astarte or Tanit. Twin hills called San Marco and Santa Teresa formed the acropolis, ringed by rectangular-block walls and cisterns cut to catch scarce rainwater. Rome captured Cossyra for good in 217 BCE, and its Punic-cut cisterns still held water for residents in 117 CE.

Nora was Sardinia's first Phoenician settlement, founded by the 8th century BCE, later growing into a full Punic and then Roman city. The Nora Stone, unearthed there in 1773, carries the oldest known Phoenician writing found on the island. A storm in 1889 exposed a buried tophet and remains of a temple to Tanit. Roman builders raised baths, a theater, and mosaic-floored houses directly over much of the old Punic quarter, so a visitor in 117 CE walked a working Roman port town built atop its Phoenician predecessor.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the archaeological site of Nora, Sardinia

properties.modern_location: San Giovanni di Sinis, Cabras, Sardinia, Italy
properties.notes: Tharros was founded by Phoenician settlers in the 8th century BCE on Sardinia's Sinis peninsula and passed through Carthaginian and then Roman hands without ever being abandoned. Its tophet, atop the hill of Su Muru Mannu, held cremation urns of sacrificed infants and animals from the 7th century BCE onward. Unlike most Phoenician cities on the island, Tharros stayed continuously inhabited for another millennium, only emptying in the 11th century CE when Saracen raids drove its people inland to found Oristano.

Phoenicians founded Sulci around 770 BCE, and it grew into one of Sardinia's most important trading ports before Carthage absorbed it in the 6th century BCE. Its tophet, where cremated infant and animal remains were sealed in urns beneath carved stelae, ranks as Sardinia's best-preserved example of the practice. Rome conquered Sulci in the 3rd century BCE and joined the island to the mainland with an artificial causeway still used today. The stelae-filled sanctuary remained in the ground beneath the working Roman town in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the tophet of Sant'Antioco (ancient Sulci)

properties.notes: Tuvixeddu served as the burial ground of Phoenician-Punic Karales, now Cagliari, and ranks as the largest Punic necropolis in the Mediterranean. Between the 6th and 3rd centuries BCE, diggers cut close to 1,800 well-shaft tombs into the limestone hill, some eight meters deep, a handful preserving rare North African-style wall paintings. Rome took Karales in the First Punic War and built its own city on the same site, leaving Tuvixeddu's older tombs untouched on the city's edge through the imperial period.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Tuvixeddu necropolis, Cagliari

properties.notes: Phoenician settlers built a fortified hilltop town at Monte Sirai around 750 BCE to guard the approaches to nearby Sulci, and Carthage took direct control by 520 BCE, thickening its walls and adding a tophet by the late 4th century BCE. The children's necropolis yielded urns shaped like covered pots, packed with cremated remains, amulets, and jewelry. The entire settlement was abandoned around 110 BCE, two centuries before Trajan's reign, leaving it an empty ruin rather than a living Roman-era town.

properties.modern_location: Chia, Domus de Maria, Sardinia, Italy
properties.notes: Phoenician traders founded Bithia on Sardinia's southern tip around the 8th century BCE, and the port continued under Carthaginian and then Roman control without being abandoned in antiquity. Excavators found a monumental Punic-era statue of the dwarf god Bes near a sanctuary outside the town, alongside roughly two hundred votive clay figurines. Bes worship stayed popular into the Roman period, so the shrine that drew Punic sailors likely still drew visitors when Trajan ruled in 117 CE.

Puig des Molins served as the burial ground for Ebusus, modern Ibiza, from the mid-7th century BCE, staying in continuous use for over a thousand years through Phoenician, Punic, and Roman rule. Roughly 3,000 tombs honeycomb the hillside, most Carthaginian-style hypogea reached by a shaft into a square underground chamber. It remains the largest and best-preserved Phoenician-Punic necropolis in the western Mediterranean, and burials continued straight through 117 CE and for centuries afterward.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Puig des Molins necropolis, Ibiza

properties.notes: Phoenician settlers reached Lixus by the 7th century BCE, and Pliny the Elder later called it the most ancient Phoenician colony in the far west. Its acropolis carried a sanctuary to Melqart, the Tyrian god Romans equated with Hercules, and Greek writers placed the mythical Garden of the Hesperides here, imagining Hercules plucking golden apples from its slopes. In 117 CE the hilltop shrine still overlooked a busy fish-salting port below.

Phoenician traders set up an outpost on this archipelago by the 7th century BCE, the westernmost Phoenician foothold known in antiquity. Client-king Juba II later built a full purple-dye works here, crushing murex and purpura sea snails harvested from the surrounding rocks to make Tyrian purple, the dye that colored a Roman senator's toga stripe. The dye works were still operating under Roman provincial administration when Trajan died in 117 CE.

Phoenician traders had a presence at Tingis by around 1450 BCE, and Carthaginian colonists formally founded a counter there between 475 and 450 BCE. On the Marshan plateau above the harbor, a rock-cut necropolis of more than 100 tombs, some carved into a gorge wall, held burials in a distinctive Libyco-Phoenician style. Rome eventually made Tingis the capital of Mauretania Tingitana, and the tombs of the city's Phoenician-era predecessors remained in the ground through 117 CE.

Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded Gadir around the 11th century BCE; it endures as one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in western Europe. Shipyard workers struck its necropolis in 1887, unearthing a male anthropoid marble sarcophagus, a bearded figure clutching a pomegranate, so finely Hellenized in its carving that the find prompted the founding of the Cadiz Archaeological Museum. A matching female sarcophagus, the Lady of Cadiz, turned up nearby only in 1980. The graves span the 5th through 2nd centuries BCE, already undisturbed underground by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Phoenician anthropoid sarcophagi in the Museum of Cadiz

properties.modern_location: mouth of the Guadalhorce River, Malaga, Spain
properties.notes: Phoenician colonists built this eight-hectare town on what was then an island at the Guadalhorce river mouth no later than the 8th century BCE, one of the best-preserved Phoenician settlements in the western Mediterranean. Unlike most Iron Age Phoenician towns buried under the modern cities built on top of them, Cerro del Villar was abandoned by the 6th century BCE and never resettled. By 117 CE the site had lain empty and unknown for roughly six centuries, while nearby Malaca had grown into the real Roman-era port city.

The Laurita necropolis at Sexi holds the oldest Phoenician tombs found anywhere in the western Mediterranean, dated as early as 850 to 770 BCE. Among the grave goods were Egyptian alabaster jars carved with hieroglyphic names of pharaohs including Osorkon II, prestige gifts that traveled from the Nile through Phoenician trade networks. Sexi grew into the Roman colony Firmum Iulium Sexi, and its founders' necropolis remained in the hillside above the town through Trajan's reign.

properties.modern_location: Villaricos, Cuevas del Almanzora, Almeria, Spain
properties.notes: Phoenician settlers founded Baria in the 8th century BCE, drawn by nearby silver-bearing lead deposits and rich fishing grounds. Its cemetery at Villaricos ranks among the most extensive Phoenician necropoleis on the Iberian Peninsula, with monumental rock-cut hypogea from the 7th century BCE. A limestone funerary stele found there in 1903, inscribed for a devotee of Astarte, preserves one of the clearest Phoenician religious inscriptions recovered in Spain. Burials continued without interruption from the 6th century BCE into the 2nd century CE, spanning straight through 117 CE.

Hasdrubal the Fair founded Qart Hadasht around 227 BCE as Carthage's Iberian capital, naming it "New City" after the mother city and using its harbor to move silver from nearby mines. Two parallel ramparts of local sandstone, discovered beneath the modern city, formed the settlement's original 3rd-century-BCE wall. Rome captured the city in 209 BCE, and Augustus's later redevelopment built out well beyond this Punic perimeter, leaving the old wall's line buried and obsolete by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, the Punic wall of Cartagena

properties.notes: Phoenician colonists founded Abdera in the 8th century BCE on the Cerro de Montecristo, one of a chain of trading posts alongside Malaca, Sexi, and Baria. Punic authorities took direct control by the 4th century BCE before Rome absorbed the town at the end of the 2nd century BCE. Under Roman rule Abdera shipped out lead and iron from the nearby Sierra de Gador along with salted fish, an economy built on the trade routes its Phoenician founders first established.

Sidonian kings Eshmunazar II and Bodashtart founded this sanctuary to Eshmun, the Phoenician god of healing, in the 7th century BCE beside the Awali river. French excavations uncovered a monumental podium, a sacred pool for pilgrims seeking cures, and a carved bull-headed capital surviving from its colonnade. The complex kept growing under Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman patronage, gaining a Roman-style nymphaeum, and stayed in active religious use from the 7th century BCE through the 8th century CE — in 117 CE, worshippers visited a healing cult already eight hundred years old.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Bull protome capital from the Temple of Eshmun.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, a bull-protome capital from the Temple of Eshmun, Sidon

properties.notes: Carthaginian traders rebuilt an older Phoenician counter at Icosium in the early 3rd century BCE, giving it a Punic name meaning "Island of the Owls." The modern Arabic name for Algiers, al-Jazair ("the islands"), still echoes that ancient toponym nearly 2,300 years later. A Roman veteran colony was established under client-king Juba II, and Vespasian later elevated the town to full colonia status. By 117 CE, Icosium sat as a modest but functioning Roman port city built directly on its Phoenician-Punic predecessor.

Phoenician-Punic sailors carved a cliffside sanctuary to Astarte into the rock at Ras il-Wardija on Gozo's western tip, using it from at least the 4th century BCE to leave offerings before crossing open water toward North Africa. Cut into two terraces 120 meters above the sea, the complex held rock-hewn niches, cisterns, and a temple enclosure. Excavations found the sanctuary kept functioning under Roman rule, eventually gaining a Roman-style nymphaeum, and stayed active until roughly the 2nd century CE — sailors were very likely still leaving offerings there in 117 CE.

Phoenician traders settled this small island at the mouth of the Tafna river by the 7th century BCE, building a compact town beside a carved channel resembling the artificial cothon harbors Phoenician engineers built elsewhere. Excavators uncovered 114 graves in a cemetery nicknamed the Necropolis of the Lighthouse, its early Punic pottery showing direct trade links to Iberia. The colony lasted less than two centuries before being abandoned, likely by the 5th century BCE, and no later town replaced it. By 117 CE, Rachgoun had sat empty for roughly five hundred years.

Vercingetorix surrendered his sword here in 52 BCE after Caesar's double ring of siege works starved 80,000 Gauls into submission, ending organized resistance to Rome. Unlike most defeated oppida, the hilltop itself was never abandoned. A prosperous Gallo-Roman town grew directly over the ramparts, complete with a forum, theater, and bronze workshops still busy in 117 CE.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Reconstruction of the rampart of the contravallation, Alesia (7700412514).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed Caesarian siege rampart at the Museoparc Alesia, Alise-Sainte-Reine, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Bibracte ruled as capital of the Aedui, Rome's oldest Gallic allies, and hosted Caesar himself while he dictated the Commentaries on the Gallic War within its double ramparts. Its murus gallicus walls once enclosed 200 hectares of workshops and houses. Augustus lured the population down to a new city, Augustodunum, around 15 BCE, and by 117 CE the hilltop stood empty but for a shrine and a spring still visited by the faithful.
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed murus gallicus rampart wall at Bibracte, Mont Beuvray, Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Plateau de Gergovie, near Clermont-Ferrand, France
properties.notes: Vercingetorix, an Arvernian noble raised on this very plateau, handed Caesar his only defeat of the Gallic War here in 52 BCE, driving the Roman legions off the hill with heavy losses. Excavations show dense occupation continued for another generation before the Arverni resettled downhill around 10 BCE at the new Roman town of Augustonemetum. By 117 CE the abandoned plateau stood silent, its ramparts overlooking the valley city that had replaced it.
properties.image_credit: The Plateau de Gergovie hillfort site near Clermont-Ferrand, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Caesar called Avaricum the finest town in Gaul, and its Bituriges defenders held his legions off for twenty-five days behind walls of stone and packed earth before it fell and nearly its whole population was put to the sword in 52 BCE. Rome rebuilt directly on the same ground, and by 117 CE Avaricum was a thriving provincial town with bathhouses and temples rising over the old Gallic ramparts. A later Roman wall, three meters thick with 46 towers, still traces that same hilltop today.

Corent served as an earlier capital of the Arverni before Gergovia, its plateau centered on a vast open-air sanctuary where feasters once drained thousands of wine amphorae in ritual banquets. Rome did not abandon the site: engineers rebuilt the Gallic sanctuary in stone and raised a small theater beside it. Excavators have logged more than a hundred Iron Age grain silos here, and the rebuilt sanctuary complex was still functioning in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Excavated Gallo-Roman theater built beside the Gallic sanctuary at Corent, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This Arvernian oppidum guarded the Allier valley with 600 meters of rampart enclosing 28 hectares of workshops for potters and smiths. Its most startling find is a mass grave of eight warriors buried beside eight horses in matched rows, dated to the height of Caesar's Gallic War, with no weapons or grave goods to explain the ritual. The settlement did not survive into the Roman peace, and by 117 CE the site had long since emptied out.
properties.image_credit: Excavations at the Arvernian oppidum of Gondole, Le Cendre, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Enserune sat astride the Via Domitia and grew wealthy on the wine trade between Italy and Spain for seven unbroken centuries, its hillside honeycombed with hundreds of grain silos cut into bare rock. Roman-style stone townhouses replaced Gallic huts once Narbonensis became a province. Decline set in soon after, and by 117 CE the hilltop had largely emptied as its people drifted to towns on the plain below.
properties.image_credit: Excavated house foundations and silos at the Oppidum d'Enserune, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This Durotrigan stronghold ranks among the largest hillforts in Europe, its ramparts stacked in four concentric rings enclosing 19 hectares at their Iron Age peak. Suetonius records the Second Legion storming Durotrigan hillforts like this one during the 43 CE invasion, and a mass grave of war dead found at its east gate backs the memory of conquest. Rome founded Durnovaria nearby, and Maiden Castle's earthworks sat empty through 117 CE, centuries before a small Roman temple rose inside them.
properties.image_credit: Aerial photograph of Maiden Castle's concentric Iron Age ramparts, Dorset, 1935, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Twenty years of excavation at Danebury made it Britain's best-understood hillfort, revealing hundreds of grain storage pits packed inside its single circular rampart. Occupation stretched from the sixth century BCE until around 100 BCE, when burned gates and bodies dumped in the storage pits mark a violent final chapter, long before Claudius ever landed. By 117 CE only a lone farmstead lingered inside the earthwork, already a monument to a vanished age.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Danebury Ring, Iron Age Hill Fort - geograph.org.uk - 1506378.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: The ramparts of Danebury Ring hillfort, Hampshire, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Old Oswestry guarded the Welsh Marches for the Cornovii tribe behind seven ridged ramparts, its western entrance elaborated into a maze of stone-faced banks unmatched at any other British hillfort. People had used the hilltop since the Bronze Age, but occupation ended around the time Rome founded the tribal capital of Viroconium in the valley below. By 117 CE only scattered pottery sherds hinted that anyone still climbed the abandoned ramparts.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/View to Old Oswestry hillfort from the outskirts of Oswestry town.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Old Oswestry hillfort's ramparts viewed from Oswestry, Shropshire, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Four banks of rampart ring this 7-hectare hilltop, and archaeologists found a burned Iron Age gatehouse alongside scattered weapons recalling a massacre during Rome's Claudian conquest around 50 CE. Roman soldiers occupied the hill afterward, and excavators later uncovered a Roman-period shrine built on the summit. Activity thinned once the town of Lindinis grew up at nearby Ilchester, but scattered coins and pottery show the hilltop was not empty in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: The ramparts of Cadbury Castle hillfort, South Cadbury, Somerset, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Traprain Law served as the tribal center of the Votadini, a people Rome never conquered outright but courted as allies beyond the province's northern edge. At its height the hilltop settlement sprawled across 16 hectares, and Roman brooches, glass, and coins found there show steady trade reached this far north. In 117 CE the Votadini still occupied their ancestral hill, watching a Roman frontier that had not yet hardened into Hadrian's Wall five years later.
properties.image_credit: Traprain Law, the Votadini hillfort in East Lothian, Scotland, Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Stanwick St John, North Yorkshire, England
properties.notes: Stanwick was the power base of Cartimandua, the Brigantian queen who kept Rome as an ally and once handed her rebel husband Venutius over in chains. Its earthworks eventually enclosed nearly 300 acres, among the largest defended areas in Iron Age Britain. When Venutius seized power and Rome intervened around 70 CE, legions moved the tribal capital to Isurium Brigantum at Aldborough. By 117 CE Stanwick's great ramparts stood empty across the Yorkshire countryside.
properties.image_credit: Earthwork ramparts of the Stanwick Iron Age Fortifications, North Yorkshire, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Before Colchester was a Roman colonia, Camulodunon was Britain's largest native settlement, ringed by earthwork dykes running 20 kilometers, its kings Cunobelinus and Tasciovanus striking their own gold coins here. The industrial quarter at Sheepen turned out bronze goods and pottery for trade reaching across the Channel. Rome built its fortress and colonia on ground nearby rather than atop it, and after Boudica's rebels burned the district in 60 CE, only earthwork scars remained by 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Surviving Iron Age dyke earthworks of pre-Roman Camulodunon, Lexden, Colchester, Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Prae Hill, St Albans, Hertfordshire, England
properties.notes: King Tasciovanus founded Verlamion on Prae Hill as capital of the Catuvellauni, and coins struck here carry the earliest known use of the name that became St Albans. A five-kilometer ditch called Beech Bottom Dyke, among the largest earthworks in pre-Roman Britain, still cuts across the landscape nearby. Rome founded Verulamium in the valley below rather than on the hilltop, and by 117 CE Verlamion had been abandoned for decades, its ditches silting over as the new town flourished close by.
properties.image_credit: Beech Bottom Dyke, the great defensive ditch of the Verlamion oppidum, St Albans, Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Garray, Soria, Castile and Leon, Spain
properties.notes: This Celtiberian hilltop town humiliated a string of Roman armies before Scipio Aemilianus starved it into submission in 133 BCE, walling off six miles of countryside so thoroughly that survivors burned their own homes rather than surrender. The phrase defensa numantina still means a hopeless last stand in Spanish. Augustus resettled the site as a Roman road station, and the rebuilt town of 117 CE still followed the grid of narrow streets its Celtiberian founders had laid out.
properties.image_credit: Excavated house foundations at the Celtiberian and Roman site of Numantia, Soria, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This hilltop castro once housed roughly a thousand people inside a maze of stone roundhouses, its narrow paved streets fitted with a working water and drainage system before Rome ever arrived. Augustus and Tiberius's legions absorbed the settlement rather than destroying it, and Roman-style rectangular houses soon rose beside the older round ones. Roman coins and pottery mixed with local granite carvings show the community was still adapting Roman life here in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Stone roundhouses of the castro settlement at Citania de Briteiros, Portugal, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Perched above the mouth of the Mino River, this castro grew into one of the largest hillfort settlements in northwest Iberia, its hundreds of round stone huts once home to an estimated 5,000 people. Roman-style square buildings appeared alongside the roundhouses as the community absorbed provincial customs under Augustus. The population drifted away as Rome's road network pulled trade toward the lowlands, and by 117 CE the hilltop had entered its final decades of abandonment.
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed stone roundhouses at the Castro de Santa Tecla, Galicia, Wikimedia Commons

properties.modern_location: Solosancho, Avila, Castile and Leon, Spain
properties.notes: Ulaca was the largest oppidum the Vettones ever built, its three kilometers of granite walls enclosing more than 60 hectares and the stone foundations of over 250 houses. A rock-cut sacrificial altar hewn into the bedrock still marks the site's sanctuary. Rome's conquest of the Vettones stripped the town of independence around 133 BCE, and it was fully abandoned as the new Roman town of Obila rose nearby, leaving the hilltop empty well before 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Granite walls of the Vettonian oppidum of Ulaca, Avila, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This walled hillfort of the Astur Albiones packs some eighty circular stone houses inside its acropolis wall, laid out along narrow paved streets that still survive underfoot. Rome prized the gold deposits in the surrounding hills, and imperial mining crews worked alongside the castro's own people, extending the settlement's life past the conquest. That mining operation ran into the second century CE, so the castro's stone houses were still occupied in 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Circular stone houses of the Castro de Coana hillfort, Asturias, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Celtic warbands crossed from the Balkans in the 270s BCE, and the Tectosages tribe made this fortified hilltop their capital, one of three Galatian power centers ruling deep in Anatolia by force of arms. Rome annexed the Galatian kingdom in 25 BCE and built Ancyra into the province's capital without displacing the old citadel, which still crowns the hill today. In 117 CE Roman magistrates governed Galatia from the same hilltop the Tectosages chieftains had fortified three centuries earlier.
properties.image_credit: The citadel hill of Ankara, site of the Galatian Tectosages' fortified capital, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Tavium served as the tribal capital of the Trocmi, the third of the Celtic peoples who settled Galatia after crossing from the Danube, and grew rich on caravan traffic through central Anatolia. A colossal bronze statue of Zeus stood here, so revered that Strabo singled it out by name. Rome granted the settlement formal city status around 20 BCE, and by 117 CE Tavium functioned as an active Roman road town still marking the Trocmian homeland it once ruled.

Pessinus was already Anatolia's most celebrated shrine of the mother goddess Cybele when the Tolistobogii swept in around 270 BCE and made it their capital, ruling as overlords while leaving the priesthood its independence. Rome carried Cybele's sacred black stone to the capital in 204 BCE to help win the war against Hannibal. Tiberius finished a grand new temple here, and by 117 CE Pessinus stood as a thriving Greco-Roman city still serving as the Tolistobogii's tribal seat.
properties.image_credit: The theatral area of the Pessinus sanctuary complex, Ballihisar, Turkey, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: This mountaintop settlement served as royal seat of the Celtic Kingdom of Noricum, an ally Rome never had to conquer since its kings supplied Roman legions with prized Noric steel for generations. A famous bronze youth statue found here, later copied for imperial Vienna, shows how thoroughly Roman and Celtic taste had blended on the summit before annexation in 15 BCE. Claudius moved the capital down to a new town called Virunum around 45 CE, and the mountaintop stood deserted by 117 CE.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Klagenfurt - Staudaerplatz - Kopie des Jüngling vom Magdalensberg.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Copy of the bronze Youth of Magdalensberg, found at the Celtic-Roman settlement site, Klagenfurt, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: The Celtic Scordisci fortified this bluff above the meeting of the Sava and Danube rivers in the third century BCE, and its very name is Celtic, sharing a root with Singidava elsewhere in the Balkans. Rome absorbed the Scordisci homeland by the late first century BCE and stationed the Fourth Flavian Legion on the same commanding bluff. By 117 CE a Roman legionary fortress occupied the exact hilltop the Scordisci had first fortified, guarding the Danube from that old stronghold.
properties.image_credit: Kalemegdan fortress bluff, site of the Celtic Scordisci oppidum and later Roman legionary fortress, Belgrade, Wikimedia Commons

properties.notes: Manching ranked among the largest fortified settlements in Iron Age Europe, its 7-kilometer wall enclosing 380 hectares and a population near 10,000 at the Vindelici tribe's peak. Excavators have pulled more gold coins from its soil than from any other Celtic site north of the Alps. Caesar's conquest of neighboring Gaul wrecked the trade networks the town depended on, and Manching was largely abandoned by 30 BCE, decades before Rome annexed the region as Raetia in 15 BCE.
properties.image_credit: Reconstructed eastern gate of the Manching oppidum at the Kelten und Roemer Museum, Bavaria, Wikimedia Commons
